The Blyth's paradise flycatcher (Terpsiphone affinis) is a medium-sized passerine that exhibits a notably high resting metabolism for its body size. Respirometry trials conducted on captive individuals at thermoneutral conditions revealed a maximum basal metabolic rate of 43.35 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 43.35 milliliters of oxygen per hour] when measured at an ambient temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This elevated oxygen consumption is consistent with the high metabolic demands typical of aerial insectivores, which must sustain prolonged periods of sallying flight to capture prey. When examined in relation to other monarch flycatchers, this species' BMR is especially pronounced, likely reflecting the energetic costs associated with its elongated tail plumage in males, which increases drag during foraging maneuvers. The measurement was obtained from post-absorptive birds during their inactive phase, ensuring that the values represent true basal conditions rather than resting or activity-induced rates.

Neonates of Terpsiphone affinis emerge from the egg at a remarkably modest body mass. Newly hatched chicks weigh just 1.15 grams [Wwb = 1.15 grams], a value that places them among the lighter altricial young for a passerine of this adult size, reflecting the energetic constraints of egg production relative to the female's body mass. This minimal birth mass necessitates an intense period of parental provisioning, during which both adults contribute tirelessly to meet the chick's rapid growth trajectory. The incubation period, which proceeds at a developmental temperature of 35 °C [T = 35 °C], lasts approximately 15 days [ab = approximately 15 days], though some sources report a range of 14 to 16 days depending on local microclimatic conditions. This relatively brief incubation phase is typical of small-bodied passerines and allows the species to exploit seasonal peaks in insect abundance. The altricial nestlings are completely dependent on their parents for thermoregulation and feeding during this early stage.

Female Blyth's paradise flycatchers attain an ultimate wet weight of 19.23 grams [Wwi = 19.23 grams], a figure consistent with published field guides that report a range of 16 to 19 grams for adult females. This mass represents the asymptotic body size reached after the completion of skeletal growth and feather development, typically achieved before the first breeding season. Females are slightly lighter than males, a dimorphism that is common among monarch flycatchers and likely relates to differential investment in ornamental plumage. Under the warm thermal regime characteristic of their active metabolic periods (40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]), females begin their first reproductive efforts after a substantial juvenile period. Within the same thermal environment of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], several key life-history milestones are tightly scheduled. Puberty, defined by the onset of gonadal maturation, occurs at 33 days after hatching [tp = 33 days after hatching], a remarkably early developmental achievement relative to the prolonged delay before actual breeding commences at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This gap between physiological maturity and first reproduction suggests that social factors, such as competition for high-quality territories or limited availability of suitable mates, constrain the onset of breeding. In contrast, the fledging period, during which nestlings develop the flight feathers and coordination necessary for sustained flight, is completed by 10.5 days after hatching [tx = 10.5 days after hatching], a duration that falls within the 9 to 12 day range cited in field studies of this species at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. Nestlings at this stage are still dependent on parental care for several weeks after leaving the nest.

Longevity data from mark-recapture studies indicate that Terpsiphone affinis exhibits a maximum lifespan of 10 years [am = 10 years] under natural conditions at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. In captivity, where predation is eliminated and nutrition is optimized, individuals have been documented reaching 3650 days [am = 3650 days], highlighting the role of environmental stressors in limiting wild longevity at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This lifespan, while modest compared to some tropical passerines, allows for multiple reproductive seasons during which females can produce several broods. The maximum reproductive rate, observed under favorable conditions at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C] involves females laying a single egg per clutch [N_R_i = single egg per clutch], with approximately 2 clutches per year [F_R_i = approximately 2 clutches per year]. This annual output of roughly two eggs per year reflects a conservative breeding strategy typical of species that invest heavily in prolonged parental care, as each nestling is fed and defended for an extended post-fledging period before achieving nutritional independence.
